subject: penguin
pitch: An emperor penguin chick's proud parent. Glossy blue-black back and head, a crisp white belly blending into a warm golden-yellow patch at the neck and ear, a long slender beak with an orange-pink stripe, stubby flippers held slightly out, and big black feet. A fluffy grey chick peeks out from between its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning to write a single TypeScript module using the SDK's builder API—things like joints, chains, sweeps, parts, and paint helpers—to model an adult emperor penguin around 1.1m tall alongside a fluffy grey chick, sticking to conservative, well-documented methods since I can't test the code directly.

Working out the skeleton: a hip root joint, then a spine chain running from hips up through the chest to the neck base using a catmull path, followed by a separate neck chain up to the head, so the body can be swept into an egg-like torso shape leaning slightly forward for the belly.

For coloring, I want the back dark blue-black and the belly white, so instead of using countershade (which works on up/down normals) I need a custom paint function that checks the surface normal's z-component to distinguish dorsal from ventral sides.

I also want a gold ear patch near the head sides, so I'm adding conditions checking the y-position and x-normal magnitude to place that patch correctly, while keeping unused callback parameters prefixed with underscore for type safety. Then I'll apply this same paint logic to the head sphere geometry for consistent coloring.

For the beak, I'm planning a slender sweep along a bezier curve from the head's front, considering whether to split it into separate upper and lower jaw joints for more realistic articulation, though I'm leaning toward a simpler single jaw joint parented to the head.

I'm working out the beak's coloring with paint logic that applies black everywhere except an orange-pink stripe along the top, detecting the stripe region using sweep path position and lateral angle. I'm also adding small dark eye spheres positioned relative to the head joint.

For the flippers, I'm sketching stubby wing shapes held slightly away from the body using a three-point sweep path from shoulder to tip, tapering the radius so they're flat and narrow with thickness along the normal direction and width along the binormal.

I can't easily rotate the extruded flipper outward without a proper transform, so I'll just accept it hanging vertically from the shoulder attachment point as a reasonable approximation.

For the mirrored flippers, I'm orienting both outlines the same way in the YZ plane with thickness along X so they're naturally symmetric without needing a mirror transform—just offsetting their x-position by the side sign. Now I'm thinking through the feet: simple flattened webbed triangle shapes attached at the ankle joints, kept minimal since they're just black accents against the ground.

Setting the foot's vertical center so it sits flush on the floor, with the leg bone connecting down to the ankle. For the chick, I'm thinking a fluffy grey sphere body positioned between the feet, partially peeking out, sized and placed so it sits naturally on the ground near the front of the feet.

For the fluff texture, I'm considering scattering small spheres across the chick's surface using a surface-based scatter method with a minimum distance filter, then sticking tufts onto each hit point rather than relying on textures. I'll attach the chick body as its own sphere part bound to the hips bone, positioned slightly above the floor.

Now I'm working through the body proportions: feet should sit at floor level with short legs tucked under the body, and the main torso needs to be positioned so its bottom cap sits just above the legs rather than floating or sinking into the ground. I'm adjusting the hip height and tube radius so the rounded bottom cap of the body aligns correctly with the visible leg length.

For the body shape itself, I'm defining a tapered path with radius keyframes that widen toward the belly and narrow near the neck, then placing a head joint at the top of the spine chain where the last spine segment ends, making sure the chain's named joints line up properly with where the head attaches.

Writing body cross-section function...

For coloring, I'm setting up a paint function that marks the front-facing, lower portion of the body white (chest and belly) while leaving the rest blue, using the surface normal's z-component and the y-position to distinguish the chest region.

Now I'm defining gold patches at the neck sides based on normal direction and y-range, picking out the color palette (blue-black, gold, white, beak black, feet black), and working through head sphere placement with a relative-position ear patch and matching eye geometry positioning.

I'm sketching out the beak as a swept bezier path from the head front down to a tapered tip, using radius arrays to taper the beak shape and leaving end caps rounded by default.

For coloring, I'm planning a paint function that checks sweep coordinates to mark a pink stripe near the top while keeping the rest black, and adding a separate lower mandible sweep attached to a new jaw joint parented to the head.

Now I'm positioning the chick's body between the parent's feet, peeking out from the front.

I'm placing the chick's head and tiny eye spheres with precise offsets so they protrude slightly from the body sphere, and deciding to skip a separate beak shape to save on part budget.

For texture, I'm scattering small grey spheres across the chick's surface for a fluffy look, embedding them slightly and filtering out ones pointing downward to avoid belly clutter. I'm skipping extra feet and fluff details elsewhere, keeping flippers as simple colored extrusions and attaching them to a joint along the spine chain.

I'm setting up the skeleton now: a hips root joint feeding into a three-joint spine chain built from catmull-rom points, then a head joint parented to the last spine joint, relying on default orientation inheritance rather than explicit aiming.

For the body mesh, I realize I can sweep directly from the spine chain itself rather than a separate path, since a chain's parametrization works the same way for radius functions.

Now I'm defining the paint functions for the body's color regions—white belly based on forward-facing normals and vertical position, gold patches on the neck/head sides using normal and position thresholds, being careful to keep unused paint parameters prefixed with underscore to satisfy the typechecker. I'm also working out the head sphere's local coloring logic using a position offset from its center to carve out facial detail regions.

Now I'm sketching the flipper shape as an extruded outline with a few points defining its tapered profile, adding a bevel and smoothing, with a sharp point at the tip—making sure the outline array is typed correctly so the "sharp" marker doesn't break type inference.

I'm working out the tilt direction so the flipper's tip angles slightly outward from the body, adjusting the extrude's y-direction vector based on which side (left/right) the flipper is on.

Now I'm positioning the flipper's hinge point against the body surface, calculating the body's half-width at that height using the key profile interpolation so the flipper sits embedded against the shoulder. For the feet, I'm setting up a simpler extrude in the XZ plane with straight x/y direction vectors, mirroring the outline for each side.

I'm designing a webbed foot outline with three sharp toe tips arranged in a crown shape, checking the point ordering doesn't self-intersect, then setting thin extrusion thickness and placing a leg joint bone under the hips without an aim constraint.

Now I'm connecting the leg joint to the ankle with a rigid rod, assigning explicit bone references so the foot inherits the correct joint rather than the nearest default. I'm also planning joint roles for the rig -- naming leg, wing (flipper), head, and jaw joints with unique names and appropriate parent-child relationships so the skeleton reads cleanly.

Then I'm placing the beak geometry: upper beak swept along a bezier curve bound to the head bone, lower beak bound to the jaw bone, positioned just inside the head sphere's surface with tapering radii. For coloring, I'm painting a pink stripe across the top of the upper beak based on sweep angle and position, while the lower beak gets a solid beak color -- and I'm about to start on the eyes next.

I'll scatter fluff on the chick head too, mixing the lighter and darker chick colors for variation. I'm checking proportions so everything sits properly on the ground, then settling on head/body heights roughly matching an emperor penguin's real size—around 1.1-1.2m—adjusting the head center and body top accordingly without needing to redo all the facial feature positions.

Setting up imports and the color palette for the model—blue, white, gold, beak black, pink, foot black, eye black, plus the chick's grey tones and fluff highlights—before defining the metadata export.

I'm defining the body shape with keyed radius interpolation for the egg-like profile, then writing a paint function that assigns white to the belly, gold to the neck patches, and blue elsewhere based on normal and position checks, before sweeping that profile along the spine with a sides parameter for smoother faceting.

Now I'm setting up the head joint attached to the spine, adding a sphere part for the skull with its own paint function, placing eye spheres symmetrically on each side, and starting a bezier sweep for the upper beak shape.

Moving on to the lower jaw joint and its beak sweep, then building the legs: hip joints off the hips, rod segments forming the legs down to the ankle, and extruded foot shapes attached at each side.

Now I'm working out the flippers, adding wing joints off the spine and extruding tapered flipper shapes that are thin at the tip and wider near the body, colored blue and mirrored for each side, checking that the outline geometry angles outward correctly.

For the chick, I'm placing spherical body and head parts on the hips bone, adding tiny eyes positioned relative to the head center, a small orange beak rod, and scattering fuzzy sphere tufts across the body surface using a filtered random distribution to create a fluffy texture.

Adding scattered fluff to the head too, alternating between two fluff colors for variation. Then I'm setting up the overall joint structure: a hips joint at the base, a spine chain built from a catmull curve with three named segments running up to the head, and a sweep along that spine to form the torso, making sure parenting and positions line up correctly before finalizing the build.
